feedback: If the child counts up from 6 (or from 1) rather than referring to 6+6, put 6+6 and 6+7 side by side so the single extra cube is visible, and name 6+7 as 'the double and one more'.
If the child says 6+7=14 (added two) or doubles the 7, use the two rows to show exactly ONE cube was added — steady the adjustment; no need to reteach doubles.
Probe flexibility: 'you used 6+6 to get 6+7 — could you use 7+7 instead (one less than 14)? which double is handiest here?'
activities.intendedInsight: A near-double can be derived from an adjacent known double by adjusting, instead of counting up from one.
learnerActions: Set out two rows of 6 cubes (or two ten-frames of 6) and confirm the double: 6+6=12.
Add exactly ONE more cube to one row and say the new total: 6+7=13. State it as 'the double I know, and one more'.
Repeat for 6+8 ('two more than the double, so 14') and for another double you know, e.g. 7+7=14 so 7+8=15.
Say aloud which double you used and how many you adjusted by, before giving the total.
activities.title: Near-doubles builder: the double plus one

feedback: If the child subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones, use the hundred square to show the move is one whole row back (straight up on a square with 1 in the top row; straight down on a square numbered from the bottom) — the ones digit does not change.
Counterexample to bound the rule: 'you said take away ten drops the tens digit — does take away ONE do that to 45?' (45−1=44) to check the child limits the rule to −10.
Confirm by reading the place-value cards: the tens card goes down one, the ones card is untouched.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting 10 from a two-digit number lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — and a good rule is stated with the conditions under which it holds.
learnerActions: On a hundred square (or with place-value cards), start at a two-digit number such as 45 and subtract 10; land on 35 and notice the tens digit dropped by one while the ones digit stayed the same.
Repeat from two or three other starting numbers to see the same pattern each time; state the rule: 'take away 10 drops the tens digit by one'.
Test the boundary: does taking away ONE do the same thing? Try 45−1 (which gives 44) and see it does not — so the rule is only for −10.
Say the rule in your own words AND what it does NOT cover.
activities.title: Subtracting 10 on a hundred square — and bounding the rule
